def: To adjust precisely for a particular function or accuracy.
ex: Engineers must calibrate the laboratory sensors before starting the high-precision chemical experiment.
nat: We need to calibrate the screen colors properly.

mis.bad: We calibrated about the scale.
mis.good: We calibrated the scale.
mis.why: "Calibrate" is transitive; do not use "about".

def: Showing or having an insensitive and cruel disregard for others.
ex: His callous remarks about the laid-off workers shocked everyone in the executive meeting.
nat: It was callous of him to laugh at her misfortune.

mis.bad: He was callous with the dog.
mis.good: He was callous toward the dog.
mis.why: Use "callous toward", not "with".

def: Truthful and straightforward; frank.
ex: During the exit interview, she shared candid feedback about the management style.
nat: To be candid, I am not thrilled with the proposal.

mis.bad: He was very candid about of the problem.
mis.good: He was very candid about the problem.
mis.why: Say "candid about [a topic]", without "of".

def: The quality of being open and honest in expression; frankness.
ex: I truly appreciate your candor when discussing our recent performance and team issues.
nat: She answered all the difficult questions with complete candor.

mis.bad: He spoke with much candor about.
mis.good: He spoke with great candor.
mis.why: "Candor" is a noun meaning honesty; do not add prepositions without an object.

def: To take the chance to gain advantage from something.
ex: Smart entrepreneurs always capitalize on new market trends before competitors even notice them.
nat: The team capitalized on their opponent's defensive errors.

mis.bad: We must capitalize of this chance.
mis.good: We must capitalize on this chance.
mis.why: Always use "capitalize on [something]", not "of".

def: To attract and hold the interest and attention of; charm.
ex: The keynote speaker managed to captivate the entire audience with her opening story.
nat: Her beautiful singing never fails to captivate listeners.

mis.bad: The movie captivated to me.
mis.good: The movie captivated me.
mis.why: "Captivate" is transitive; omit "to".

def: To pass down or transfer in a succession of stages or drops.
ex: A single database timeout can cascade into multiple service failures across production.
nat: Water cascaded down the rock face after the rain.

mis.bad: The errors cascaded to all the system.
mis.good: The errors cascaded throughout the system.
mis.why: Use "cascade into" or "cascade through/throughout".

def: A person killed or injured in a war or accident.
ex: Fortunately, the severe office fire caused zero casualties thanks to prompt evacuation.
nat: Small businesses were the main casualties of the recession.

mis.bad: The accident had two casualties deaths.
mis.good: The accident resulted in two casualties.
mis.why: "Casualty" already implies death or injury; do not say "casualty deaths".

def: A person or thing that precipitates an event or change.
ex: The surprising product launch served as a major catalyst for company-wide reform.
nat: Her speech was the catalyst that started the protest.

mis.bad: The new law was a catalyst of changes.
mis.good: The new law was a catalyst for change.
mis.why: Use "catalyst for", not "of".

def: To hurl or launch with great force, or move rapidly to a new level.
ex: Winning the prestigious design award helped catapult the small agency to global fame.
nat: His breakout single catapulted him into immediate international stardom.

mis.bad: The success catapulted him on the top.
mis.good: The success catapulted him to the top.
mis.why: Use "catapult [someone] to/into [a position]".

def: An event causing great and often sudden damage or suffering; a disaster.
ex: The sudden server crash proved to be an absolute catastrophe for our business.
nat: Humanitarian agencies rushed to prevent an environmental catastrophe.

mis.bad: The earthquake was a big catastrophic.
mis.good: The earthquake was a huge catastrophe.
mis.why: Use the noun "catastrophe", not the adjective "catastrophic", after "a".

def: To provide what is needed or desired by a group or event.
ex: Our internal development platform was designed to cater to both novices and experts.
nat: The hotel can easily cater for large corporate conferences.

mis.bad: The menu caters for vegetarians people.
mis.good: The menu caters to vegetarians.
mis.why: Use "cater to [someone's needs]" or "cater for [an event]".

def: Firm conviction that something is the case; something that cannot be doubted.
ex: Nobody can predict the exact future of artificial intelligence with absolute certainty.
nat: There is no certainty that mortgage interest rates will drop soon.

mis.bad: I have the certainty that we will win.
mis.good: I am certain that we will win.
mis.why: It is more natural in English to say "I am certain" rather than "I have the certainty".

def: To attest or confirm in a formal or legal statement.
ex: The board must formally certify all test results before releasing the medical device.
nat: Two independent physicians had to certify the cause of death.

mis.bad: He was certified like a cloud architect.
mis.good: He was certified as a cloud architect.
mis.why: Use "certify as [a role]", not "like".

def: Compelling attractiveness or charm that can inspire devotion in others.
ex: His natural charisma made it remarkably easy to win over skeptical corporate investors.
nat: She has immense personal charisma on television and the stage.

mis.bad: He has a lot of charism.
mis.good: He has a lot of charisma.
mis.why: The English noun is "charisma" (stress on the second syllable), not "charism".

def: Exercising a compelling charm that inspires devotion in others.
ex: She is a charismatic leader who inspires her team through every difficult deadline.
nat: A charismatic speaker can make even dry subjects sound interesting.

mis.bad: He is a very carismatic politician.
mis.good: He is a very charismatic politician.
mis.why: Spelled with "ch" and pronounced /k/, not /tʃ/.

def: Relating to the assistance of those in need, or generous and lenient.
ex: The tech company donates a charitable contribution to local public schools annually.
nat: She tried to be charitable when judging her colleague's flawed design.

mis.bad: They founded a charitative institution.
mis.good: They founded a charitable organization.
mis.why: The English adjective is "charitable", not "charitative".

def: The base frame of a motor vehicle or other wheeled conveyance.
ex: Technicians inspected the metal chassis of the electric vehicle after the crash test.
nat: The lightweight aluminum chassis helps improve fuel efficiency significantly.

mis.bad: The car chassi was damaged.
mis.good: The car chassis was damaged.
mis.why: Spelled "chassis" in singular and plural; the final "s" is silent in the singular (/ˈʃæsi/).

def: To hold something dear; feel or show great affection for.
ex: I cherish every single memory of traveling across South America with my family.
nat: They cherish their independence and refuse all corporate buyout offers.

mis.bad: She cherishes for her grandmother's watch.
mis.good: She cherishes her grandmother's watch.
mis.why: "Cherish" is transitive and takes no preposition.

def: Courteous behavior, especially that of a man towards women; gallantry.
ex: Some people believe that chivalry is dead, but simple polite gestures still matter.
nat: His quiet chivalry impressed everyone at the formal company banquet.

mis.bad: His cavalheirism was appreciated.
mis.good: His chivalry was appreciated.
mis.why: Do not invent "cavalheirism"; the English word is "chivalry" (pronounced with /ʃ/).

def: A thick, solid piece of something, or a substantial amount.
ex: We broke the massive database migration script into smaller chunks for safety.
nat: A large chunk of our annual budget goes toward cloud hosting.

mis.bad: I ate a chunk of bread (meaning a slice).
mis.good: I ate a slice of bread.
mis.why: Use "slice" for bread; "chunk" is an irregular, thick, or bulky block.

def: A roughly circular line, route, or movement, or a complete electrical path.
ex: A blown fuse interrupted the electrical circuit and turned off the laboratory lights.
nat: The tennis champion returned to the competitive tournament circuit this spring.

mis.bad: The electricity circuit is broken.
mis.good: The electrical circuit is broken.
mis.why: Use the adjective "electrical circuit", not "electricity circuit".

def: To move continuously through a closed system, or distribute widely.
ex: The manager will circulate the draft proposal to all team members by tomorrow.
nat: Blood circulates throughout the body carrying oxygen to every vital organ.

mis.bad: Rumors are circulating around about him.
mis.good: Rumors are circulating about him.
mis.why: Avoid redundant "around about"; use "circulate about" or simply "circulate".

def: Movement to and fro or around something, especially that of fluid or information.
ex: Regular morning walking improves blood circulation and helps reduce daily cognitive fatigue.
nat: The local magazine has a print circulation of fifty thousand copies.

mis.bad: Cold hands can mean poor blood circularity.
mis.good: Cold hands can mean poor blood circulation.
mis.why: Use "circulation" for movement of blood, air, or papers; not "circularity".

def: A fact or condition connected with or relevant to an event or action.
ex: Under no circumstance should you share your production database password with anyone.
nat: Due to unforeseen financial circumstances, the wedding had to be postponed.

mis.bad: In this circumstance we cannot proceed.
mis.good: Under these circumstances we cannot proceed.
mis.why: The idiomatic preposition in English is "under these circumstances", rarely "in".

def: To quote as evidence for or justification of an argument.
ex: Please cite all relevant academic sources in the footnotes of your final paper.
nat: The report cited several key factors behind the sudden economic slowdown.

mis.bad: He cited about the article in his thesis.
mis.good: He cited the article in his thesis.
mis.why: "Cite" is transitive; do not use "about".

def: A quotation from or reference to a book, or an official commendation or summons.
ex: The police officer issued a formal traffic citation for exceeding the speed limit.
nat: His published academic paper received over one hundred scholarly citations this year.

mis.bad: Check the text citation of the book.
mis.good: Check the citation from the book.
mis.why: Say "a citation from [a work]" or "citation of [an author]".

def: Relating to a city, town, or the duties of citizens.
ex: Voting in municipal elections is an essential civic duty for every responsible citizen.
nat: The mayor organized a civic reception for the visiting international diplomats.

mis.bad: They demonstrated civic pride in city.
mis.good: They demonstrated civic pride in their city.
mis.why: Say "civic pride in [something]".

def: A person not in the armed services or the police force.
ex: The international peace treaty strictly prohibits military strikes against any civilian target.
nat: After twenty years in the navy, he found civilian life surprisingly quiet.

mis.bad: He is a civil now.
mis.good: He is a civilian now.
mis.why: Use the noun "civilian" for a non-military person, not "civil" (which is an adjective).

def: The quality of being clear, easily understood, or transparent.
ex: Her concise summary brought much needed clarity to the complex technical discussion.
nat: The microphone captured every word of his speech with astonishing clarity.

mis.bad: I need more clearness about this rule.
mis.good: I need more clarity about this rule.
mis.why: Prefer "clarity" over "clearness" in formal and professional contexts.

def: To grasp something tightly with one's hand, or fasten with a small device.
ex: She fastened the golden clasp of her necklace securely before leaving home.
nat: He clasped his daughter's hand tightly while walking across the busy street.

mis.bad: She clasped to the railing.
mis.good: She clasped the railing.
mis.why: "Clasp" is transitive; do not insert "to".

def: To arrange or order by classes or categories.
ex: The algorithm can classify incoming customer feedback into positive, neutral, or negative.
nat: Government agencies classify sensitive security documents according to strict confidentiality levels.

mis.bad: We classified the emails in three folders.
mis.good: We classified the emails into three categories.
mis.why: Use "classify into [categories]", not "in".

def: The action or process of classifying something according to shared characteristics.
ex: Security clearances depend heavily on the official classification level of the confidential documents.
nat: The biological classification system groups organisms into kingdom, phylum, and species.

mis.bad: The team needs a better classification of tasks.
mis.good: The team needs better task classification.
mis.why: Avoid awkward literal Portuguese phrasing like "classification of tasks".

def: The state or quality of being clean or being kept clean.
ex: Hospital inspection standards require absolute cleanliness in every operating room at all times.
nat: Good personal cleanliness prevents the spread of seasonal viral infections in schools.

mis.bad: We must check the clean of the room.
mis.good: We must check the cleanliness of the room.
mis.why: Use the noun "cleanliness", not the adjective "clean".

def: A phrase or opinion that is overused and betrays a lack of original thought.
ex: Saying "think outside the box" has become an annoying corporate cliché nowadays.
nat: The plot of the action film was full of tired romantic clichés.

mis.bad: His argument is a very clichéd thing.
mis.good: His argument is a tired cliché / His argument is clichéd.
mis.why: Use "cliché" as a noun or "clichéd" as an adjective without adding "thing".

def: To hold on tightly to someone or something, physically or emotionally.
ex: Desperate investors tend to cling to losing stocks in hope of a recovery.
nat: Wet cotton shirts tend to cling uncomfortably to your skin in humidity.

mis.bad: He clings in his old habits.
mis.good: He clings to his old habits.
mis.why: Always use "cling to [something]", not "in".

def: Relating to the observation and treatment of patients, or coldly detached.
ex: The hospital launched a clinical trial to test the novel cancer therapy.
nat: His voice had a clinical detachment when describing the horrifying traffic accident.

mis.bad: The doctor opened a clinical private.
mis.good: The doctor opened a private clinic.
mis.why: Use the noun "clinic" for the building; "clinical" is strictly an adjective.

def: Rough or loose in texture or grain, or crude and vulgar.
ex: Use coarse salt to season the steak before grilling it over charcoal.
nat: His coarse jokes made several colleagues feel uncomfortable during the team dinner.

mis.bad: The sand has a very course texture.
mis.good: The sand has a very coarse texture.
mis.why: Do not confuse "coarse" (rough) with "course" (class/direction).

def: To persuade someone gradually or gently to do something.
ex: The senior engineer tried to coax the legacy server into running smoothly.
nat: She managed to coax the shy kitten out from under the car.

mis.bad: He coaxed her to eating vegetables.
mis.good: He coaxed her into eating vegetables.
mis.why: Use "coax someone into doing something", not "to doing".

def: To exist at the same time or in the same place peacefully.
ex: Different programming paradigms can coexist peacefully within a large modern software architecture.
nat: Can traditional print media coexist with fast-paced digital social networks indefinitely?

mis.bad: The two groups cannot coexist with each other together.
mis.good: The two groups cannot coexist peacefully.
mis.why: Avoid redundant phrases like "coexist together with each other".

def: Relating to the mental processes of perception, memory, judgment, and reasoning.
ex: Excessive multitasking often causes severe cognitive overload and diminishes daily work productivity.
nat: Puzzles and foreign language learning provide valuable cognitive benefits for older adults.

mis.bad: He has strong cognitives abilities.
mis.good: He has strong cognitive abilities.
mis.why: Adjectives in English never take a plural "-s".

def: The action or state of sticking together tightly; unity.
ex: Clear communication builds strong team cohesion during stressful quarterly product release cycles.
nat: The essay lacked logical cohesion between its third and fourth argument paragraphs.

mis.bad: The text has no cohesive.
mis.good: The text has no cohesion.
mis.why: Use the noun "cohesion", not the adjective "cohesive".

def: To occur at or during the same time, or correspond in nature.
ex: Our product release date will coincide with the largest developer conference in Europe.
nat: My personal opinions on code quality coincide closely with company architectural standards.

mis.bad: Our vacation coincides to the holiday.
mis.good: Our vacation coincides with the holiday.
mis.why: Always use "coincide with", not "to".

def: A remarkable concurrence of events or circumstances without apparent causal connection.
ex: Running into my former manager in Tokyo was a truly bizarre coincidence.
nat: By an extraordinary coincidence, we both booked seats on the exact same train.

mis.bad: It was an incredible coincidency.
mis.good: It was an incredible coincidence.
mis.why: The English noun ends in "-ce" ("coincidence"), not "-cy".

def: A person who works jointly on an activity or project with others.
ex: She is a trusted collaborator who regularly contributes valuable code to open source.
nat: He thanked his academic collaborators in the acknowledgments section of the study.

mis.bad: He is an employee collaborator of the company.
mis.good: He is an employee of the company / a company collaborator.
mis.why: In English, "collaborator" usually means a creative or research partner; for employees, say "colleague" or "employee".

def: To fall down or give way suddenly; fail completely and suddenly.
ex: A sudden power surge caused the entire network infrastructure to collapse yesterday.
nat: The marathon runner collapsed from extreme physical exhaustion right past the finish.

mis.bad: The bridge collapsed down yesterday.
mis.good: The bridge collapsed yesterday.
mis.why: Do not add "down"; "collapse" already means fall down.

def: To hit with force when moving towards something; come into direct conflict.
ex: Two shipping vessels almost collided in the dense fog near the harbor entrance.
nat: Their conflicting personal ambitions inevitably collided during the contentious executive meeting.

mis.bad: The car collided against a tree.
mis.good: The car collided with a tree.
mis.why: Use "collide with", not "against".

def: An instance of one moving object or person striking violently against another.
ex: The automated safety system prevented a head-on collision on the icy mountain highway.
nat: A routing collision occurred when two services claimed the same internal domain.

mis.bad: They had a collision of cars.
mis.good: They had a car collision / car crash.
mis.why: Use "car collision" or "car accident" instead of literal "collision of cars".

def: Used in ordinary or familiar conversation; not formal or literary.
ex: Avoid using overly colloquial phrases in formal corporate emails or job interviews.
nat: "Gonna" and "wanna" are common colloquial contractions used in everyday spoken English.

mis.bad: He spoke in a very coloquial manner.
mis.good: He spoke in a very colloquial manner.
mis.why: Notice the double "l": "colloquial".

def: To take action to reduce, suppress, or stop something bad or undesirable.
ex: The department introduced strict security measures to combat rising phishing attacks effectively.
nat: Drinking hot tea and resting can help combat early symptoms of seasonal flu.

mis.bad: We must combat against inflation.
mis.good: We must combat inflation.
mis.why: "Combat" is transitive; do not use "against".

def: To join or merge to form a single unit or whole.
ex: We should combine both approaches to achieve maximum reliability and overall system performance.
nat: Hydrogen and oxygen combine under proper laboratory conditions to produce pure water.

mis.bad: I want to combine with you to study.
mis.good: I want to get together with you to study.
mis.why: Do not use "combine with you" for "combinar com alguém"; use "arrange with" or "get together".

def: The process of burning something; rapid chemical combination of a substance with oxygen.
ex: Internal combustion engines produce carbon emissions that harm the environment and public health.
nat: Spontaneous combustion caused the dry pile of oily cleaning rags to ignite.

mis.bad: The combustion of gas is fast.
mis.good: Gas combustion is fast.
mis.why: Use compound nouns like "gas combustion" rather than literal "combustion of".

def: To recall and show respect for someone or something in a ceremony.
ex: The monument was erected to commemorate the brave soldiers who defended the city.
nat: Every November, schools commemorate the signing of the historic armistice treaty.

mis.bad: We commemorated my birthday with a party.
mis.good: We celebrated my birthday with a party.
mis.why: Use "celebrate" for festive events like birthdays; "commemorate" is specifically for honoring historical memory.

def: To begin; start.
ex: The keynote presentation will commence promptly at ten in the main auditorium.
nat: Construction on the cross-country railway is scheduled to commence early next spring.

mis.bad: The meeting will commence at Monday.
mis.good: The meeting will commence on Monday.
mis.why: Use "on Monday", not "at Monday".

def: To praise someone or something formally or officially.
ex: The director took time to commend the security team for preventing data theft.
nat: I commend your dedication to mastering professional spoken English through daily practice.

mis.bad: The manager commended to the intern.
mis.good: The manager commended the intern.
mis.why: "Commend" is transitive; do not insert "to".

def: Deserving praise or approval.
ex: Her quick response during the production outage was truly commendable and saved money.
nat: Reaching an advanced language level within one intensive year is a commendable achievement.

mis.bad: His work was very commendative.
mis.good: His work was commendable.
mis.why: The English adjective is "commendable", not "commendative".

def: Concerned with or engaged in commerce; intending to make a profit.
ex: The startup struggled to achieve commercial viability during its first two operating years.
nat: Television networks run fewer commercial advertisements during overnight cultural broadcasts.

mis.bad: They opened a commercial store.
mis.good: They opened a retail store / commercial business.
mis.why: Say "retail store" or "shop" rather than "commercial store".

def: The state or quality of being dedicated to a cause, activity, or promise.
ex: Learning fluent English requires daily commitment and constant exposure over many months.
nat: She could not attend the dinner due to a prior professional commitment.

mis.bad: I have a compromise with my doctor today.
mis.good: I have an appointment with my doctor today.
mis.why: In English, "compromise" means reaching mutual concessions; a scheduled meeting or promise is a "commitment" or "appointment".

def: A raw material or primary agricultural product that can be bought and sold.
ex: In the modern digital economy, private personal data has become a valuable commodity.
nat: Global market fluctuations heavily impact countries whose economies depend on agricultural commodities.

mis.bad: The hotel offers many commodities (meaning amenities).
mis.good: The hotel offers many amenities.
mis.why: Do not confuse "commodity" (goods/raw material) with Portuguese "comodidade" ("amenity" or "convenience").

def: Not unusual; ordinary; happening often.
ex: Remote work and virtual meetings have become commonplace across global technology companies.
nat: Smartphone photography has made instant document scanning commonplace for students everywhere.

mis.bad: Electric cars are very commonplace of seeing.
mis.good: Electric cars are commonplace nowadays.
mis.why: Use "commonplace" directly as a predicate adjective; do not add "of seeing".

def: A state of confused and noisy disturbance.
ex: A loud argument in the lobby caused a huge commotion among hotel guests.
nat: The puppy caused quite a commotion when he burst into the dining room.

mis.bad: There was a big comotion on the street.
mis.good: There was a big commotion on the street.
mis.why: Spelled with double "m": "commotion".

def: Willing, eager, or able to talk or convey information readily.
ex: Language courses should prioritize real communicative competence over memorizing obscure grammatical rules.
nat: He became noticeably more communicative once he felt welcomed by his project teammates.

mis.bad: She has great communication skills and is very comunicative.
mis.good: She has great communication skills and is very communicative.
mis.why: Spelled with "mm": "communicative".

def: Closely and neatly packed together; dense; taking up little space.
ex: The new laptop features a remarkably compact design without sacrificing computational power.
nat: The historical town center is compact enough to explore entirely on foot.

mis.bad: The office is very compact of space.
mis.good: The office is very compact.
mis.why: Omit "of space"; "compact" already conveys spatial density.

def: Able to be compared or of equivalent quality or size.
ex: The performance of our open model is comparable to proprietary alternatives on benchmarks.
nat: Salaries for senior engineers in Berlin are now comparable with those in London.

mis.bad: The results are comparable of each other.
mis.good: The results are comparable to each other.
mis.why: Always use "comparable to" or "comparable with", not "of".

def: Perceptible by comparison; relative; or involving comparison.
ex: The analyst conducted a comparative study of healthcare costs across ten developed nations.
nat: After months of chaotic restructuring, the engineering team now works in comparative peace.

mis.bad: They live in comparative rich.
mis.good: They live in comparative luxury / comfort.
mis.why: Follow "comparative" with a noun (comfort, ease) or use "comparatively" before an adjective.

def: A state in which two things are able to exist or work together without problems.
ex: Always verify hardware compatibility before purchasing new memory modules for your workstation.
nat: Astrological sign compatibility has zero scientific backing when predicting long-term relationship success.

mis.bad: There are some incompatibilities between the parts.
mis.good: There are compatibility issues between the parts.
mis.why: In English, we say "compatibility issues" or "compatibility problems".

def: To force or oblige someone to do something.
ex: Urgent client demands often compel software developers to postpone scheduled code refactoring.
nat: Financial hardship compelled her to take a second job on weekend evenings.

mis.bad: The law compels drivers to wearing helmets.
mis.good: The law compels drivers to wear helmets.
mis.why: Use "compel someone to + base verb", not "-ing".

def: Evoking interest, attention, or admiration in a powerfully irresistible way.
ex: The founder presented a compelling business case that convinced even conservative venture investors.
nat: Her debut novel is a compelling story of resilience against overwhelming odds.

mis.bad: His presentation was very compellent.
mis.good: His presentation was compelling.
mis.why: The English adjective is "compelling", not "compellent".

def: To give something, typically money, in recognition of loss, suffering, or injury.
ex: The airline offered travel vouchers to compensate passengers for the eight-hour flight delay.
nat: Nothing can truly compensate for the loss of a close family member.

mis.bad: The company will compensate the damage to you.
mis.good: The company will compensate you for the damage.
mis.why: Use "compensate [someone] for [loss]", not "compensate the damage to someone".

def: The ability to do something successfully or efficiently.
ex: The interview process evaluated both technical competence and general cultural fit within teams.
nat: Language competence develops naturally through consistent, comprehensible immersion in realistic contexts.

mis.bad: He showed great competence on programming.
mis.good: He showed great competence in programming.
mis.why: Use "competence in [a field]", not "on".

def: To produce a list or book by collecting information from various sources, or convert code into machine language.
ex: The build system takes several minutes to compile the entire backend application codebase.
nat: She spent three months compiling data for her doctoral dissertation.

mis.bad: I need to compile together these files.
mis.good: I need to compile these files.
mis.why: Avoid redundant "together"; "compile" already means gather together.

def: A computer program that translates code written in a high-level language into machine code.
ex: The modern Rust compiler generates extremely fast and memory-safe machine code automatically.
nat: Optimization flags passed to the compiler can significantly reduce binary file size.

mis.bad: The compilator showed two syntax errors.
mis.good: The compiler showed two syntax errors.
mis.why: In English, the program is a "compiler", not a "compilator".

def: Showing smug or uncritical satisfaction with oneself or one's achievements.
ex: Market leaders often become complacent and fail to notice aggressive new digital startups.
nat: We cannot afford to grow complacent about software security practices.

mis.bad: He is complacent with customers (meaning pleasing).
mis.good: He is accommodating with customers.
mis.why: False cognate: "complacent" means self-satisfied or smug, NOT "prestativo" or "gentil" (accommodating/pleasant).

def: To add to something in a way that enhances or improves it.
ex: The new user interface will complement the existing database architecture very well.
nat: Crisp white wine complements fresh seafood dishes perfectly.

mis.bad: She complemented him on his shirt (spelling error).
mis.good: She complemented the decor / She complimented his shirt.
mis.why: Do not confuse "complement" (complete/enhance) with "compliment" (praise).

def: Combining in such a way as to enhance or emphasize the qualities of each other.
ex: The two co-founders possess complementary skills in technical engineering and corporate marketing.
nat: Our services are complementary to existing cloud solutions.

mis.bad: They offer complementary coffee (meaning free).
mis.good: They offer complimentary coffee (free).
mis.why: Distinguish "complementary" (enhancing/matching) from "complimentary" (free or flattering).

pt: tez / aspecto da pele / tom geral
def: The natural color, texture, and appearance of a person's skin, especially of the face.
ex: Drinking plenty of water and eating fresh fruit can improve your facial complexion.
nat: The sudden resignation of the prime minister changed the whole political complexion.

mis.bad: He has a strong body complexion (meaning build).
mis.good: He has a strong physical build.
mis.why: False cognate: "complexion" refers to facial skin appearance, not body frame or build ("build/physique").

def: The state of being involved with others in an illegal activity or wrongdoing.
ex: Internal auditors uncovered evidence of executive complicity in the offshore accounting fraud.
nat: Silence in the face of injustice often signals tacit complicity.

mis.bad: They share a nice complicity of friendship.
mis.good: They share a close bond of friendship.
mis.why: In English, "complicity" usually implies involvement in wrongdoing; for positive friendship closeness use "bond" or "camaraderie".

def: Consisting of many interconnecting parts or elements; intricate; difficult to analyze.
ex: Explaining microservice distributed tracing can feel complicated to entry-level software developers.
nat: Their tax situation became far more complicated after buying foreign real estate.

mis.bad: It is very complicated of understand.
mis.good: It is very complicated to understand.
mis.why: Use "complicated to + base verb", not "of + verb".

def: To write or create a work of art, or constitute a whole.
ex: She sat down quietly in the evening to compose a thoughtful cover letter.
nat: Water is composed of two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.

mis.bad: He composed about a letter to the client.
mis.good: He composed a letter to the client.
mis.why: "Compose" is transitive; do not insert "about".

def: A person who writes music, especially as a professional occupation.
ex: The famous film composer spent three months writing the emotional orchestral movie soundtrack.
nat: Beethoven is widely regarded as one of history's greatest classical composers.

mis.bad: He is a great lyric composer (for songs).
mis.good: He is a great songwriter / lyricist.
mis.why: In English, "composer" usually refers to instrumental/orchestral music; for pop songs use "songwriter".

def: The state or feeling of being calm and in control of oneself.
ex: The team lead maintained his composure despite intense pressure from demanding corporate clients.
nat: It took several deep breaths for her to regain her composure.

mis.bad: He lost his calm and composure control.
mis.good: He lost his composure.
mis.why: Do not add "control"; "composure" already means self-possession and calm control.

def: To make something bad worse, or combine to form a whole.
ex: Ignoring early minor software bugs will only compound technical debt over coming months.
nat: Interest compounds monthly on this high-yield corporate savings account.

mis.bad: Stress compounded to her sickness.
mis.good: Stress compounded her sickness.
mis.why: "Compound" is transitive when meaning worsen; omit "to".

def: To consist of; be made up of.
ex: The steering committee will comprise senior representatives from engineering, design, and marketing.
nat: The entire international federation comprises over fifty independent national member organizations.

mis.bad: The team is comprised of ten people (debated).
mis.good: The team comprises ten people / is composed of ten people.
mis.why: Strict traditional usage prefers "comprises ten people" rather than "is comprised of".

def: To calculate or reckon an amount or number mathematically or via software.
ex: Modern GPUs can compute complex matrix operations much faster than older chips.
nat: Algorithms compute the optimal flight path based on real-time weather data.

mis.bad: The app computes out the total.
mis.good: The app computes the total.
mis.why: Do not add "out"; "compute" takes a direct object.

def: The action of mathematical calculation, or the use of computers.
ex: Deep neural network model training requires an enormous amount of cloud-based computation.
nat: Parallel computation allows distributed clusters to process petabytes of sensor data simultaneously.

mis.bad: We did the computation of numbers.
mis.good: We did the calculation / computation.
mis.why: Say "computation" for automated mathematical operations.

def: To keep from sight; hide; prevent from being known or noticed.
ex: Malware often uses clever encryption techniques to conceal its malicious payload from antivirus.
nat: He tried hard to conceal his disappointment after losing the tennis match.

mis.bad: She concealed the truth from of him.
mis.good: She concealed the truth from him.
mis.why: Use "conceal [something] from [someone]", without "of".

def: Capable of being imagined or grasped mentally.
ex: The engineering team prepared contingencies for every conceivable failure scenario during deployment.
nat: It is conceivable that autonomous electric drones will handle local parcel deliveries soon.

mis.bad: That error is not conceivable of happening.
mis.good: It is hardly conceivable that such an error would happen.
mis.why: Use "conceivable that..." rather than "conceivable of happening".

def: To focus one's full attention or mental effort on an object or activity.
ex: Loud open-plan offices make it difficult for programmers to concentrate on complex algorithms.
nat: I need an hour of absolute quiet so I can concentrate properly.

mis.bad: I cannot concentrate myself with noise.
mis.good: I cannot concentrate with noise.
mis.why: In English, "concentrate" is not reflexive; never say "concentrate myself".

def: The action or power of focusing one's attention or mental effort.
ex: High caffeine intake can temporarily improve concentration, but quality sleep remains fundamentally essential.
nat: The industrial city has a high concentration of chemical manufacturing plants.

mis.bad: He broke my concentration on reading.
mis.good: He broke my concentration while I was reading.
mis.why: Say "break someone's concentration" or "disturb concentration".

def: The action of conceiving a plan or idea, or becoming pregnant.
ex: Our initial conception of the mobile app changed drastically after direct user feedback.
nat: I have absolutely no conception of how much cloud storage that database requires.

mis.bad: I had the conception that you were sick.
mis.good: I had the impression / idea that you were sick.
mis.why: In everyday contexts, use "idea" or "impression"; "conception" means a broad mental construct.

def: Relating to or based on mental concepts or theoretical ideas.
ex: Before writing any code, the team created a clear conceptual design model.
nat: The candidate demonstrated strong conceptual understanding of distributed operating system architectures.

mis.bad: He has a conceptual problem (meaning fundamental).
mis.good: He has a conceptual misunderstanding.
mis.why: Say "conceptual understanding/framework" rather than vague "conceptual problem".

def: To bring something to an end, or arrive at an opinion by reasoning.
ex: We can conclude from the quarterly benchmark metrics that page load times improved.
nat: The international economic summit will conclude on Friday afternoon with a press briefing.

mis.bad: I concluded my college last month.
mis.good: I finished / graduated from college last month.
mis.why: Do not use "conclude" for finishing school; say "finish college" or "graduate".

def: Serving to settle an issue or prove something definitively.
ex: The clinical study provided conclusive evidence that daily walking lowers heart disease risk.
nat: Fingerprint analysis gave investigators conclusive proof of the suspect's presence.

mis.bad: The test was not very concludent.
mis.good: The test was not conclusive.
mis.why: The English adjective is "conclusive", not "concludent".

def: To be of the same opinion; agree.
ex: All senior software architects concur that migrating to serverless will reduce infrastructure bills.
nat: I concur with my colleague's assessment regarding the potential security risks.

mis.bad: I concur to your idea.
mis.good: I concur with your idea.
mis.why: Use "concur with [someone/opinion]", not "to".

def: To express complete disapproval of, typically in public; censure.
ex: Human rights organizations worldwide strongly condemn the wrongful imprisonment of peaceful political dissidents.
nat: Inspectors had to condemn the old timber bridge due to severe structural rot.

mis.bad: He was condemned by stealing.
mis.good: He was condemned for stealing / convicted of stealing.
mis.why: Use "condemn [someone] for [behavior]" or "convict of [a crime]".

def: To make something denser or more concentrated; express in fewer words.
ex: Please condense your twenty-page research proposal into a concise three-page executive summary.
nat: Water vapor condenses on cold window panes during freezing winter mornings.

mis.bad: Condense down this article for me.
mis.good: Condense this article for me.
mis.why: Avoid saying "condense down"; "condense" already implies shortening.

def: To accept and allow behavior that is considered morally wrong or offensive.
ex: Our university does not condone any form of academic plagiarism or cheating whatsoever.
nat: Staying silent when teammates are bullied seems to condone toxic workplace culture.

mis.bad: The school condones with bad behavior.
mis.good: The school condones bad behavior.
mis.why: "Condone" is transitive; do not use "with".

def: To organize and carry out an activity; direct, or behave in a specified way.
ex: The security team will conduct a thorough vulnerability assessment of the cloud infrastructure.
nat: The students conducted themselves with outstanding maturity during the overseas field trip.

mis.bad: We must conduct a research about it.
mis.good: We must conduct research on it.
mis.why: "Research" is uncountable in English; say "conduct research", not "a research".

def: To have discussions; exchange opinions; or grant a title, degree, or benefit.
ex: The judges will confer privately before announcing the winner of the coding hackathon.
nat: The honorary university degree was conferred upon the Nobel peace laureate.

mis.bad: Let me confer to my manager first.
mis.good: Let me confer with my manager first.
mis.why: Use "confer with [someone]" to mean consult.

def: A formal statement admitting that one is guilty of a crime or error.
ex: The suspect signed a written confession after investigators presented undeniable digital video proof.
nat: I have a minor confession to make: I ate the last slice of cake.

mis.bad: He made a confess to the police.
mis.good: He made a confession to the police.
mis.why: Use the noun "confession", not the verb "confess".

def: Intended to be kept secret or private.
ex: All medical records and patient communications must remain strictly confidential under federal law.
nat: Please keep this salary information confidential until official contracts are signed.

mis.bad: Keep this file in confidential.
mis.good: Keep this file confidential.
mis.why: Use the adjective directly: "keep [something] confidential", not "in confidential".

def: The state of keeping or being kept secret or private.
ex: Every new employee must sign a formal confidentiality agreement regarding proprietary corporate algorithms.
nat: Client doctor confidentiality protects individuals seeking therapy for mental health conditions.

mis.bad: They signed a term of confidentials.
mis.good: They signed a confidentiality agreement / NDA.
mis.why: In English, we say "confidentiality agreement" or "non-disclosure agreement".

def: An arrangement of elements in a particular form, figure, or combination.
ex: A simple misconfigured routing rule in the network configuration took down the gateway.
nat: The database configuration allows up to two thousand concurrent persistent client connections.

mis.bad: Check the server configure.
mis.good: Check the server configuration.
mis.why: Use the noun "configuration" for the settings; "configure" is the verb.

def: To keep or restrict someone or something within certain limits of space or topic.
ex: Please confine your remarks during the meeting to the current fiscal quarter budget.
nat: A lingering knee injury confined the athlete to bed for several weeks.

mis.bad: Confine your question about the topic.
mis.good: Confine your questions to the topic.
mis.why: Use "confine [something] to [a topic]", not "about".

def: To state or prove the truth, correctness, or validity of something.
ex: The client will confirm their hotel reservation as soon as travel dates finalize.
nat: Subsequent laboratory experiments confirmed the researcher's original revolutionary hypothesis.

mis.bad: Please confirm to me your arrival time.
mis.good: Please confirm your arrival time with me.
mis.why: "Confirm" takes a direct object ("confirm your arrival time").

def: The action of confirming something or the state of being confirmed.
ex: You will receive an automated confirmation email immediately after booking your flight ticket.
nat: We are still awaiting written confirmation from the landlord regarding the lease.

mis.bad: I need a confirm of the flight.
mis.good: I need a confirmation of the flight.
mis.why: Use the noun "confirmation", not the verb "confirm".

def: To comply with rules, standards, or laws; behave according to societal expectations.
ex: All new building designs must conform strictly to municipal fire and earthquake regulations.
nat: Teenagers often feel immense social pressure to conform to their peers' clothing styles.

mis.bad: The device conforms with safety standards.
mis.good: The device conforms to safety standards.
mis.why: Use "conform to [a standard/rule]".

def: Compliance with standards, rules, or laws; behavior in accordance with socially accepted conventions.
ex: Blind conformity to company tradition can stifle creative innovation and hinder growth opportunities.
nat: The software was tested for conformity with European international privacy standards.

mis.bad: We must ensure the conform of the code.
mis.good: We must ensure the conformity of the code.
mis.why: Use the noun "conformity", not "conform".

def: To meet someone face to face with hostile or argumentative intent, or face a difficulty.
ex: Good managers politely confront performance issues early rather than letting resentments build up.
nat: You must confront your deepest fears if you wish to grow personally.

mis.bad: She confronted with her coworker about the gossip.
mis.good: She confronted her coworker about the gossip.
mis.why: "Confront" is transitive; do not use "with" before the person.

def: A hostile or argumentative meeting or situation between opposing parties.
ex: Avoiding unnecessary emotional confrontation helps maintain healthy working relationships among team members.
nat: The border dispute escalated into a dangerous armed confrontation between both armies.

mis.bad: There was a violent confront on the street.
mis.good: There was a violent confrontation on the street.
mis.why: Use the noun "confrontation", not "confront".

def: To make someone bewildered or perplexed, or mistake one person/thing for another.
ex: Using similar variable names across different modules can easily confuse junior software developers.
nat: People often confuse authentic Brazilian Portuguese pronunciation with European Portuguese accents.

mis.bad: I am confusing with this rule.
mis.good: I am confused by this rule.
mis.why: Use "-ed" for people feeling bewildered: "I am confused", not "I am confusing".

def: Uncertainty about what is happening, intended, or required.
ex: Vague error messages create unnecessary confusion and frustration for end users of apps.
nat: There was total confusion at the airport when all digital departure screens failed.

mis.bad: The news made a big confuse.
mis.good: The news caused a lot of confusion.
mis.why: Use the noun "confusion", not "confuse".

def: To praise someone and express pleasure at that person's success or luck.
ex: We gathered in the lobby to congratulate Sarah on her promotion to director.
nat: I want to congratulate you on passing your demanding medical board exams.

mis.bad: I congratulate you for your wedding.
mis.good: I congratulate you on your wedding.
mis.why: Use "congratulate [someone] on [an achievement/event]", not "for".

def: An opinion or conclusion formed on the basis of incomplete information.
ex: His controversial claims about the security vulnerability are pure conjecture without verifiable data.
nat: Astronomers engaged in lively conjecture about the unusual signal from deep space.

mis.bad: That is just a conjecturation.
mis.good: That is just conjecture.
mis.why: The English noun is "conjecture", not "conjecturation".

def: A word used to connect clauses or sentences, or the simultaneous occurrence of events.
ex: Use a coordinating conjunction like "and" or "but" to link two independent clauses.
nat: The software tool was developed in conjunction with leading university medical researchers.

mis.bad: We worked in conjunction to the university.
mis.good: We worked in conjunction with the university.
mis.why: The collocation is "in conjunction with", not "to".

def: To overcome and take control of a place or people by use of military force, or overcome an obstacle.
ex: Consistent daily pronunciation practice will help you conquer fear of speaking in meetings.
nat: Ancient Roman legions marched across vast continents to conquer diverse foreign kingdoms.

mis.bad: He conquered a new job yesterday.
mis.good: He landed a new job / got a new job.
mis.why: False cognate: "conquer" means overcome or defeat by force; for getting a job or winning someone's heart use "land", "get", or "win over".

def: The assumption of control of a place or people by use of military force.
ex: The historical book details the brutal Spanish conquest of the ancient Inca empire.
nat: Scaling Mount Everest was the ultimate mountaineering conquest of his adventurous youth.

mis.bad: Her new car was a great conquest for her.
mis.good: Her new car was a great achievement for her.
mis.why: In Portuguese "conquista" often means personal achievement; in English use "achievement" or "milestone", not "conquest".

def: An inner feeling or voice viewed as acting as a guide to the rightness or wrongness of one's behavior.
ex: He refused to falsify the report because his moral conscience would not allow it.
nat: She had a guilty conscience after forgetting her mother's sixty-fifth birthday celebration.

mis.bad: He lost the conscience in the accident.
mis.good: He lost consciousness in the accident.
mis.why: Do not confuse "conscience" (moral sense of right and wrong) with "consciousness" (state of being awake).

def: Wishing to do one's work or duty well and thoroughly.
ex: She is a conscientious engineer who thoroughly tests every single edge case before merging.
nat: A conscientious student reviews vocabulary notes every single morning without missing days.

mis.bad: He is very conscient about his work.
mis.good: He is very conscientious about his work.
mis.why: Use "conscientious" (careful/diligent), not "conscient" (which does not exist in English).

def: Aware of and responding to one's surroundings; awake, or having knowledge of something.
ex: Make a conscious decision to pause and breathe deeply when feeling workplace stress.
nat: The patient remained fully conscious throughout the entire minor laser eye surgery.

mis.bad: I am conscious about the risks.
mis.good: I am conscious of the risks / aware of the risks.
mis.why: Use "conscious of [something]", or prefer "aware of".

def: The state of being awake and aware of one's surroundings; the awareness of something.
ex: The injured cyclist slowly regained consciousness after the paramedics arrived at the scene.
nat: Meditation retreats aim to expand self awareness and elevate everyday human consciousness.

mis.bad: He regained his conscience after the fall.
mis.good: He regained consciousness after the fall.
mis.why: Remember: "consciousness" is wakefulness/alertness; "conscience" is moral sense.

def: Following continuously; in unbroken or logical sequence.
ex: The online retail store recorded record sales profits for four consecutive fiscal quarters.
nat: She won three consecutive national championship titles during her impressive athletic career.

mis.bad: He worked for five days consecutives.
mis.good: He worked for five consecutive days.
mis.why: Adjectives must precede the noun in English: "consecutive days", not "days consecutives".

def: Following as a result or effect.
ex: The factory closure and consequent job losses severely damaged the local regional economy.
nat: A sharp drop in oil supply caused consequent price spikes at petrol stations.

mis.bad: The pollution has a consequent effect.
mis.good: The pollution has a resulting / consequent effect.
mis.why: Use "consequent" as an attributive adjective meaning "resulting".

def: Averse to change or innovation and holding traditional values; or moderate and cautious.
ex: Our financial advisor recommended a conservative investment strategy focused on low-cost index funds.
nat: She gave a conservative estimate of project completion, predicting mid-November rather than October.

mis.bad: He gave a conservator estimate.
mis.good: He gave a conservative estimate.
mis.why: The English adjective is "conservative", not "conservator" (which is a legal guardian).

def: To protect something from harm or destruction, or use it sparingly to prevent loss.
ex: During hot summer heatwaves, citizens are encouraged to conserve electricity and water carefully.
nat: Athletes learn to pace themselves properly to conserve physical energy for late sprints.

mis.bad: We need to conserve our money in bank.
mis.good: We need to save our money in the bank.
mis.why: Use "save money" for personal finance; "conserve" is typically for natural resources, energy, or historical heritage.

def: Notably large in size, amount, or extent.
ex: The open source project attracted considerable attention after trending on social developer channels.
nat: She invested a considerable amount of personal savings into starting her consulting firm.

mis.bad: He made a considerative effort.
mis.good: He made a considerable effort.
mis.why: The adjective is "considerable", not "considerative".

def: Characterized by careful thought for the rights and feelings of others.
ex: It was very considerate of him to bring gluten-free snacks for the team.
nat: Please be considerate of your neighbors and turn down loud music after ten.

mis.bad: He was very considerable with me.
mis.good: He was very considerate toward me.
mis.why: Do not confuse "considerable" (large/substantial) with "considerate" (thoughtful/kind).

def: Careful thought, typically over a period of time, or thoughtfulness towards others.
ex: We must give careful consideration to accessibility guidelines when designing modern mobile applications.
nat: Thank you for taking my application into serious consideration during the hiring round.

mis.bad: After much considers, I decided to leave.
mis.good: After much consideration, I decided to leave.
mis.why: Use the noun "consideration", not "considers".

def: Conformity in the application of something, typically that which is necessary for the sake of logic, accuracy, or fairness.
ex: Consistent practice and habit consistency matter far more than irregular bursts of intense study.
nat: Check the consistency of the batter before pouring it into the hot waffle iron.

mis.bad: We need more consistence in the tests.
mis.good: We need more consistency in the tests.
mis.why: The noun in English is "consistency", not "consistence".

def: To comfort someone at a time of grief or disappointment.
ex: She tried to console her crying friend after the disappointing job interview result.
nat: Nothing anyone said could console the grieving mother after the tragic loss.

mis.bad: He consoled to his brother.
mis.good: He consoled his brother.
mis.why: "Console" is transitive; do not use "to".

def: The process of making something physically stronger or more solid, or combining things.
ex: The recent corporate consolidation merged three regional offices into one central headquarters building.
nat: Debt consolidation allows consumers to combine multiple high-interest credit cards into one monthly payment.

mis.bad: They announced the consolidate of the teams.
mis.good: They announced the consolidation of the teams.
mis.why: Use the noun "consolidation", not the verb "consolidate".

def: Standing out so as to be clearly visible; attracting notice or attention.
ex: The red error banner was conspicuous against the clean white layout of the page.
nat: He felt very conspicuous wearing a bright yellow tuxedo to the minimalist gallery opening.

mis.bad: She tried not to be conspicuous of herself.
mis.good: She tried not to be conspicuous.
mis.why: Do not add "of herself"; "conspicuous" is an adjective used directly.

def: A secret plan by a group to do something unlawful or harmful.
ex: Spreading baseless conspiracy theories online undermines trust in legitimate scientific and medical institutions.
nat: Two corrupt politicians were convicted of conspiracy to commit federal mail fraud.

mis.bad: They participated in a conspiration.
mis.good: They participated in a conspiracy.
mis.why: The English noun is "conspiracy", not "conspiration".

def: Occurring continuously over a period of time; remaining the same over time.
ex: Software development requires constant learning because frameworks and tools evolve at rapid speed.
nat: The constant dripping of the kitchen faucet kept me awake all through the night.

mis.bad: I need a constant feedback.
mis.good: I need constant feedback.
mis.why: "Feedback" is uncountable; do not use "a" before "constant feedback".

def: A component part of something, or a member of a constituency who can vote.
ex: Water and carbon dioxide are basic constituent parts of many living organic systems.
nat: The senator received hundreds of angry letters from constituents regarding the controversial tax vote.

mis.bad: Sugar is a constituent of the recipe.
mis.good: Sugar is a component / ingredient in the recipe.
mis.why: Use "ingredient" for cooking; "constituent" is scientific or political.

def: To be a part of a whole; combine to form a whole, or be equivalent to.
ex: Twelve completed credit units constitute a full-time academic workload at most American universities.
nat: Under state law, driving without a valid license constitutes a serious criminal misdemeanor.

mis.bad: These changes constitute into a danger.
mis.good: These changes constitute a danger.
mis.why: "Constitute" is transitive; do not add "into".

def: To build or erect something, or form an idea or theory by bringing elements together.
ex: The civil engineers plan to construct a resilient suspension bridge across the bay.
nat: The philosopher spent years constructing a rigorous theoretical framework for modern ethics.

mis.bad: They constructed down the old wall.
mis.good: They tore down the old wall.
mis.why: To take down, use "tear down" or "demolish"; "construct" only means build.

def: The building of something, typically a large structure, or the industry of building.
ex: Heavy highway construction delayed our airport shuttle by nearly forty-five frustrating minutes yesterday.
nat: The modern office building is still under construction and will open in November.

mis.bad: The road is on construction now.
mis.good: The road is under construction now.
mis.why: Always say "under construction", never "on construction".

def: To interpret a word or action in a particular way.
ex: Do not construe my honest critical feedback as a lack of personal appreciation.
nat: His extended silence during the emergency negotiation was construed as silent agreement.

mis.bad: She construed to my words as an insult.
mis.good: She construed my words as an insult.
mis.why: "Construe" takes a direct object + "as", without "to".

def: A person who provides expert advice professionally in a specific field.
ex: The board hired an independent management consultant to evaluate corporate workflow and efficiency.
nat: She earns a high hourly rate working as a freelance cybersecurity consultant.

mis.bad: I spoke with a consultee about the problem.
mis.good: I spoke with a consultant about the problem.
mis.why: Use "consultant" for the expert giving advice; "consultee" is the one receiving advice.

def: The action or process of formally discussing something, or a meeting with an expert.
ex: Book an online consultation with a physician before starting any intense new diet.
nat: Public consultation is required before the council approves major urban transport development projects.

mis.bad: I have a medical consult tomorrow.
mis.good: I have a doctor's appointment / medical consultation tomorrow.
mis.why: In English, an appointment with a doctor is usually a "doctor's appointment" or formal "consultation", not "a consult".

def: Showing a high degree of skill and flair; complete or perfect.
ex: He handled the high-stakes negotiation with consummate skill, earning the client's lasting respect.
nat: She played the complex piano sonata with consummate ease and extraordinary grace.

mis.bad: He is a consummated professional.
mis.good: He is a consummate professional.
mis.why: When used as an adjective, the form is "consummate" (not "-ed").
